title: Composition versus inheritance (has-a vs is-a)
hook: When you build a service, you usually wire up collaborators instead of extending a giant base class. C# lets you inherit from only one class, so choosing composition early keeps your design flexible.

blocks.text: **Composition** means your type *has* other objects — you store them in fields and call them through interfaces. **Inheritance** means your type *is a* specialized version of a base type — you extend a parent class and reuse its members. In a microservice worker, composition is the default: inject an `IAttemptStore`, an `IBus`, and a `IClock` rather than subclassing `BaseWorker`.

entries.plainDefinition: Building a type by combining other objects (has-a). Dependencies are injected or created inside the type.
Deriving a new class from a base class (is-a). The derived type gets the base's accessible members.
entries.example: `class LtiHandler : AuthHandler` — LtiHandler is a kind of AuthHandler.

entries.plainDefinition: The place in your application where all dependencies are wired together — usually the host or startup code.

blocks.text: Deep inheritance trees couple every derived type to a constructor chain and a protected surface you must keep forever. In production services, that makes versioning painful: changing the base class can break every child. Composition lets you swap implementations — swap Redis for SQL, swap RabbitMQ for an in-memory bus — without touching the worker's class hierarchy. C# reinforces this: you get **one** base class, so wasting it on infrastructure is expensive.

blocks.title: The interview sentence
blocks.body: Say: "I inherit for polymorphism I own; I compose for infrastructure I replace." Then point at a real worker you have shipped, not a textbook diagram.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Ask: is this a genuine is-a relationship?
items.body: If `LtiHandler` truly is an `AuthHandler` with shared validation steps, inheritance may fit. If the worker just needs to call a store, that is has-a — use composition.

items.title: Prefer interfaces for replaceable dependencies
items.body: Declare `IAttemptStore` and `IBus` as constructor parameters. The worker depends on contracts, not concrete types.

items.title: Keep hierarchies small and sealed
items.body: If you do inherit, seal derived types when the set is closed. A sealed `LtiHandler` on an abstract `AuthHandler` is a common production pattern.

items.title: Wire everything at the composition root
items.body: The host registers implementations. The worker never chooses between Redis and SQL — it just calls the interface.

blocks.title: BaseService anti-pattern
blocks.body: A `BaseService` that grows logging, HTTP, caching, and database helpers becomes a dumping ground. Every derived service inherits baggage it does not need. Extract shared behavior into small, focused services or extension methods instead.

blocks.title: Subclassing to tweak one method
blocks.body: If you subclass just to override one method, consider a strategy object or delegate instead. In C#, every subclass consumes your single base-class slot and adds a compatibility promise.

blocks.text: Design interviews test whether you can **refactor a brittle hierarchy into composable parts** without breaking callers. The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) says a derived type must honor the base contract — if `OidcHandler` throws where `AuthHandler` promised success, inheritance was the wrong tool. Composition follows the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP): high-level `AttemptWorker` depends on `IAttemptStore`, not `SqlAttemptStore`. In C# you get **one** base-class slot — wasting it on infrastructure (`BaseService`) blocks a future genuine is-a (like `TokenParser`). Inheritance also ships a **virtual surface** every derived type inherits; changing the base recompiles and retests every child. How to prove it in production: count how many files change when you rename a `protected` helper on `BaseService` versus swapping an `IAttemptStore` registration in `Program.cs`. The composition change is one line in the host; the inheritance change is a cascade across every derived service.

snippet.explanation: Lines 2–6: inheritance shares an algorithm but couples every notifier to the base constructor chain. Lines 9–14: composition extracts `INotifier` — the worker depends on the contract. Line 17: swapping to `SqsNotifier` is a one-line DI registration, not a new subclass hierarchy. This is the refactor pattern senior design interviews expect.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying "inheritance is always bad" or "inheritance is always good" — both miss the tradeoff. Claiming C# supports multiple base classes — it does not. Proposing `BaseService` with logging, HTTP, and cache for every microservice — that is the anti-pattern interviewers flag immediately. Strong answer: compose infrastructure through interfaces at the composition root; inherit only for genuine is-a with a small sealed hierarchy; one base class is precious — do not waste it on cross-cutting concerns.

interviewTakeaways: Composition is has-a via constructor injection; inheritance is is-a with one base class and a virtual compatibility surface.
Prefer composition when behavior varies by replaceable infrastructure (store, bus, notifier); inherit for closed polymorphic families (auth handlers).
In production, swapping an interface registration in Program.cs is one line; changing a protected base helper recompiles every derived service.

60s: Compose collaborators through interfaces at the composition root. Inherit only for genuine is-a with a small sealed hierarchy. C# gives one base class — do not waste it on BaseService. LSP: derived types must honor the base contract. Design interviews want you to refactor deep hierarchies into INotifier-style composition.
Follow-up: refactor a BaseService with logging, HTTP, and cache into constructor-injected interfaces without breaking callers.
commonPitfalls: Saying inheritance is always wrong or always right — that shallow answer gets rejected because LSP and closed handler hierarchies exist.
Strong answer: compose infrastructure; inherit for sealed polymorphic families; one base class is a scarce resource in C#.
BaseService that accumulates logging, HTTP, caching, and database helpers — every derived service inherits baggage it never asked for.
Subclassing to override one method when a strategy delegate or interface would swap behavior without consuming the base-class slot.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript historically piled behavior on prototypes. Modern JS and TypeScript services compose modules the same way C# workers compose interfaces.
TypeScript mixins fake multiple inheritance. C# uses interfaces plus composition; there is no mixin keyword.
